claims.text: High-entropy nanoalloys can remain structurally and chemically stable at high temperatures.
Rapid entropy-driven stabilization suppresses atomic rearrangements in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Extended high-temperature dwell times overcome kinetic barriers associated with interfacial strain.
Overcoming kinetic barriers permits local chemical ordering and segregation.
Local ordering and segregation compromise structural and chemical stability.
The proposed initial material consists of equiatomic, chemically disordered, multicomponent nanoparticles.
Dwell time can be varied while composition and peak temperature are held constant to isolate the effect of thermal exposure duration.
The proposed high-temperature regime is 700°C to 1000°C.
Surface and interfacial strain in nanoscale particles slows atomic diffusion.
At short dwell times, configurational entropy and strain-related kinetic constraints preserve a chemically disordered state.
Extended dwell times allow diffusion-driven short-range ordering and elemental segregation.
Short-dwell samples will retain a more disordered and structurally stable state than extended-dwell samples.
Extended-dwell samples will exhibit more chemical ordering or segregation than the short-dwell baseline.
Extended-dwell samples will show reduced structural stability relative to the short-dwell baseline.
The prediction applies from 700°C to 1000°C when nanoscale and surface or interfacial strain effects are significant.
The response may depend on alloy-specific diffusion kinetics and particle-size distribution.
XRD, TEM, and APT can be used to compare ordering, morphology, structural integrity, and local chemical segregation between dwell-time conditions.
Failure of extended dwell time to produce any measurable increase in ordering, segregation, or structural deterioration relative to the short-dwell control would falsify the proposed mechanism.
